title: Florentines
subtitle: lacy caramel biscuits with fruit and nuts, dipped in dark chocolate
excerpt: Florentines are thin, lacy biscuits made from caramelised cream, butter, and a mixture of dried fruit and nuts. They are baked in pools on a tray and spread into irregular rounds. The flat side is dipped in dark chocolate and left to set.
sourceNotes: Despite the Italian name, Florentines are a French confection. They are a standard of continental patisserie and British chocolate shops.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keep in an airtight tin for up to a week. Good as a gift.

content.text: The mixture will spread during baking. If any rounds merge into each other, reshape them with a round cutter immediately after they come out of the oven -- they are soft and pliable for a minute or two. Work fast. Use a palette knife to lift them cleanly from the tray before they stick.

items.prepNote: use a mix of glacé cherries (halved), flaked almonds, and mixed candied peel -- about 50g of each
use 100g dark chocolate (70%), broken into pieces, for coating

content.text: Heat the oven to 180C. Line two baking sheets with baking paper or silicone mats.
Melt the butter and cream with the sugar in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring. Bring to the boil and boil for 1 minute. Remove from heat.
Stir in the flour, then the fruit and nut mixture. Mix well.
Place teaspoonfuls on the baking sheets, leaving plenty of space. They will spread to about 8cm rounds. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until golden at the edges.

Reshape with a cutter if needed. Leave to cool completely. Melt the dark chocolate over a bain-marie or in short bursts in a microwave. Spread over the flat side of each florentine. Leave chocolate-side up to set.

items.symptom: Florentines stick to the tray and break when lifted
items.cause: Not fully cooled before lifting, or tray was not lined.
items.fix: Use good baking paper or a silicone mat. Wait until completely cold before lifting. A palette knife under each one helps.

items.cause: Chocolate was not in temper when applied.
items.fix: Melt gently to no more than 50C, then stir in a few unmelted pieces to cool. This tempers the chocolate and gives a shiny result.

content.text: Florentines are a staple of European patisserie and appear in good chocolate shops across Britain at Christmas. They are a gift biscuit -- beautiful, fragile, and clearly made with care. Despite the name, they are French in origin, possibly developed in Paris in the 19th century. They represent the point where confectionery and biscuit-making overlap.
